procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a trial court in Bihar since the Patna High Court heard a criminal appeal.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated April 5, 1966, of the Patna High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 602 of 1963.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Patna High Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 602 of 1963. The text suggests the High Court upheld a conviction and sentence under s. 147 and s. 304 read with s. 149, without considering the question as to who was actually in possession of the plot at the time of the occurrence. The High Court observed that the question of possession was immaterial and that the appellants party were members of an unlawful assembly, as both sides were determined to vindicate their rights by show of force or use of force.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court heard the case as Criminal Appeal No. 203 of 1966, after granting special leave to appeal. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether the respondents could be convicted under Section 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code.

facts: The respondents were in possession of a plot of land with mahua trees.
The deceased persons (Ramdhari and Ramswarup) and their party were attempting to commit theft of the mahua fruits from this land.
The respondents' party assembled to prevent this theft.
In the ensuing conflict, Ramdhari and Ramswarup were killed.
The prosecution could not establish which specific respondents were armed with fatal weapons (bhalas) or which of them inflicted the fatal wounds.
law: To convict a person under Section 302 (murder) read with Section 149 (unlawful assembly), the prosecution must prove that the accused was a member of an 'unlawful assembly'.
An assembly is only 'unlawful' if its common object is one of the unlawful purposes defined in the Indian Penal Code.
An assembly whose common object is to exercise the right of private defense of property is not an unlawful assembly.

For vicarious liability under Section 149, the offence (murder) must have been committed in prosecution of the common object of the assembly, or must be an act that the members knew was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object.
application: The Court determined that the respondents' assembly was not an 'unlawful assembly' because its common object was to prevent the theft of fruits from their land, which is a lawful exercise of the right of private defense of property.
The Court found that the common object of the assembly was to prevent theft, not to kill the deceased.
The murders were not committed in prosecution of this common object. Instead, the individuals who actually killed the victims exceeded the right of private defense.

Because the murders were not part of the common object, and were not an act the members knew was likely to occur, the other members of the assembly could not be held constructively or vicariously responsible for the murders.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the respondents could not be convicted under Section 302 read with Section 149 because their assembly was not 'unlawful'; its common object was the lawful act of defending their property against theft. The murders were not committed in prosecution of this common object, so the respondents could not be held constructively liable for them.

issue.issue_text: Whether the respondents could be convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.

facts: The respondents were part of a group preventing two individuals, Ramdhari and Ramswarup, from stealing mahua fruits from land one of the respondents possessed.
In the ensuing confrontation, Ramdhari and Ramswarup were killed.
The prosecution could not establish which specific respondents were armed with fatal weapons (bhalas) or who inflicted the fatal wounds.
law: To convict a person under Section 302 (murder) read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, the prosecution must prove that all the accused shared a 'common intention' to commit murder.
application: The court determined that the common intention of the respondents was to prevent the theft of the fruits, which was a lawful exercise of their right of private defense of property.
The court found that there was no evidence to establish a common intention to murder Ramdhari or Ramswarup.

The individuals who actually killed the victims exceeded the group's common intention and their right of private defense. Their actions were considered individual acts, not part of a shared plan to murder.
Since a common intention to murder was not established, the respondents could not be held constructively liable for murder under Section 34.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 because the prosecution failed to prove that the respondents shared a common intention to commit murder; their established common intention was only to prevent theft.

issue.issue_text: Whether the question of possession of the plot at the time of the occurrence was material for determining the guilt of the accused.

facts: A violent confrontation occurred over the collection of mahua fruits from trees on a plot of land, resulting in the death of two people from the prosecution party.
The High Court found that one of the accused respondents was in lawful possession of the plot of land at the time of the incident.
The High Court also found that the deceased and their party were committing theft of the fruits, which gave the respondents the right of private defence of their property.
law: Under the Indian Penal Code, a person has a right of private defence of their property against an act of theft.
An assembly of people is only considered an "unlawful assembly" if its common object is unlawful.
A person can only be held constructively liable for a crime (like murder under s. 302) committed by another member of an assembly under s. 149 if they were part of an "unlawful assembly."
The object of preventing the commission of theft in the exercise of the right of private defence is a lawful object.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that the question of who possessed the land was the critical starting point for the entire legal analysis.
Since it was established that the respondents were in possession, the actions of the deceased's party constituted theft.
This act of theft triggered the respondents' right to private defence of their property.
Therefore, the common object of the respondents' assembly was to prevent theft, which is a lawful object.
Because the assembly's common object was lawful, it could not be classified as an "unlawful assembly."

Without an unlawful assembly, the charge of constructive liability for murder under s. 302 read with s. 149 could not be sustained against the group, even if individual members exceeded the right of private defence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the question of possession was material because it determined the legality of the accused's common object. Since the accused were in possession, their object was the lawful defence of their property against theft. This meant their group was not an "unlawful assembly," which was a necessary element to convict them as a group for the murders committed by individual members.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the respondents could be convicted under Section 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code.
appellant_arguments: The accused persons knew that there was a likelihood of murders being committed in the prosecution of their common object.
respondent_arguments: The common object was only to prevent the prosecution party from collecting mahua, not to commit murder.
The respondents were in lawful possession of the property and the prosecution party's attempt to collect the mahua was high-handed, justifying their actions.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the respondents could be convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
appellant_arguments: The assailants inflicted the injuries on the victims with the common intention of murdering them.
respondent_arguments: The common intention to murder the victims was not established.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the question of possession of the plot at the time of the occurrence was material for determining the guilt of the accused.
appellant_arguments: The violent acts of the accused resulting in death were the primary issue, irrespective of who possessed the land. (inferred)
respondent_arguments: The question of possession was crucial, as they were in lawful possession and their actions were aimed at preventing the prosecution party from trespassing and taking produce from the land.

cases.principle: An assembly cannot be designated as an unlawful assembly if its object is to defend property by the use of force within the limits prescribed by law. The assertion of a right of private defence within legal limits does not fall within the expression 'to enforce any right or supposed right' under the fourth clause of s. 141 of the Indian Penal Code.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An assembly cannot be designated as an unlawful assembly if its object is to defend property by the use of force within the limits prescribed by law.
obiter: It is an incorrect application of the law to use the word 'vindicate' to include cases in which a party is forced to maintain or defend their rights.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: As it had been found that the land in question was in the possession of one of the respondents, the object of the respondents' party was to prevent the commission of theft of the fruits in exercise of their right of private defence of property. This object was not unlawful. While those who killed the victims exceeded the right of private defence and may be individually responsible, the murders were not committed in prosecution of the common object of the assembly, nor were they an outcome the members knew to be likely. Therefore, the respondents cannot be held constructively responsible for the murders.
legal_tests_applied: In order to attract the provisions of s. 149 the prosecution must establish that there was an unlawful assembly and that the crime was committed in prosecution of the common object of the assembly.

Under the fourth clause of s. 141 an assembly of five or more persons is an unlawful assembly if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is to commit any mischief or criminal trespass, or other offence.
An assembly could not be designated as an unlawful-assembly if its object was to defend property by the use of force within the limits prescribed by law.
why_appellant_lost: The prosecution failed to establish that the assembly was unlawful because its object was to prevent theft in the exercise of the right of private defense of property, which is not an unlawful object.

The prosecution failed to prove that the common object of the assembly was to kill the victims. The court found, 'Nor is it possible to say that their .common object was to kill Ramdhari and Ram-swarup.'

The prosecution could not prove that the murders were a likely consequence of the common object. The court held the murders 'were not committed in prosecution of the common object of the assembly or were such as the members of the assembly knew to be likely to be committed in prosecution of the common object.'

The prosecution failed to establish a common intention to murder, which is necessary for a conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34. The court stated, 'Intention to murder Ramdhari or Ramswarup is not established, they cannot be convicted under s. 302 read with· . ~. 34.'
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the respondents were in possession of the property, which was a material fact. 'We have found that respondent Chandradeo was in possession of plot no. 1311 and the mahua trees standing thereon.'

Because they were in possession, their objective was lawful. 'The object of the respondent's party was to prevent the commission of theft of the mhua fruits in exercise of their right of private defence of property. This object was not unlawful.'

The court distinguished between the individual acts of those who committed the murders and the common object of the group. 'Those who killed them exceeded the right of private defence and may be individually held responsible for the murders. But the murders were not committed in prosecution of the common object of the assembly...'
The respondents could not be held constructively liable for murder under Section 149 because the assembly was not unlawful and murder was not the common object.
policy_considerations: In a case where the accused person could invoke the right of private defence it is manifest that no charge of rioting under s. 147 or s. 148, Indian Penal Code can be established.

If any accused person had exceeded the right of private defence in causing death or injury, it is open to the prosecution to prove the individual assault and hold that particular accused person responsible, rather than applying constructive liability to the entire group whose initial object was lawful.
